title: Everyone Gets a Seat at the Table: A Kahoa Thanksgiving
h1_html: Everyone gets a seat at the table
description: Our family coffee farm in Kenya fed us, educated us and held three generations together. This Thanksgiving, that's the table we want to share with you.
summary: Thanksgiving isn't a Kenyan holiday, but its heart is how I grew up: one coffee farm feeding, educating and holding together a whole extended family. Today we're scattered across the world and still close, and that's the welcome we want Kahoa to give everyone.
excerpt: One coffee farm fed us, educated us and kept a big family close across three generations. That's the table we want to share.
author: martin-kibuthu

body_html:
A holiday I didn't grow up with, and a feeling I did

Thanksgiving isn't a Kenyan holiday. I didn't grow up with turkey, parades or football on the TV. But the first time I really understood what it's about, a day set aside to gather your people around one table and say thank you, it felt like home.

Because that's how I grew up. Not on one day a year, but every season, around one coffee farm.

The farm that fed all of us

More than 35 years ago, my grandfather, Jeremiah Kibuthu, planted coffee on a hillside in the Kenyan highlands. He was a teacher and a farmer, and he raised nine children. Those children had children of their own, and before long there were a lot of us.

That farm carried every one of us. Coffee put food on the table. It paid for our schooling. It covered the needs of the whole extended family, not just one household. When the harvest was good, everybody felt it. When it was hard, everybody felt that too.

You learn something when your whole family depends on the same rows of trees. Nobody eats alone. Nobody's success is only theirs. If you got an education, the farm helped pay for it, which means your grandparents, your aunts and uncles, and everyone who picked a cherry helped pay for it.

When your whole family depends on the same rows of trees, nobody eats alone.

Little buckets, red cherries and a lot of patience

Some of my earliest memories are of walking the farm with my grandmother, a thermos of tea packed for lunch and a small bucket for each of us kids. She taught us to pick only the red cherries, the ripe ones. My sisters and I turned it into a race, of course.

A new coffee tree takes years before it gives you its first real harvest. So coffee teaches you patience whether you want it or not. You plant for the people who come after you. My grandfather planted trees whose coffee would feed grandchildren he hadn't met yet. I think about that a lot now.

Scattered across the world, still at the same table

Today, my family is spread out all over the world. Cousins, aunts, uncles, brothers and sisters, everyone chasing their own passion in their own city. On paper, we've never been further apart.

But we're still close. Closer than you'd expect for a family this big and this far-flung. I really believe it's because of where we started. When something has fed you, educated you and held you together for decades, that bond doesn't disappear when you board a plane. Distance changed our addresses. It didn't change who we are to each other.

When I started Kahoa here in Austin, my family showed up. They put on the polos, stood at the booth with me and poured coffee for strangers like they'd been doing it all their lives.

Why everyone gets a seat at our table

That's what I want Kahoa to feel like. Not just a coffee brand, but a family table with room for one more chair.

It doesn't matter where you're from, what you do, or whether you've ever heard of the Kenyan highlands. When you drink our coffee, you're drinking something that fed and raised a family for three generations. In Swahili we say karibu. It means welcome. Come in, sit down, have a cup. You're family now.

That's how we try to serve at every festival, office party and wedding with the coffee cart, and in every bag we ship. Same welcome, same seat at the table.

This Thanksgiving

If your family is all around you this week, soak it up. If they're scattered like mine, call the one you haven't talked to in a while. And if you know someone who's far from home this year, pull up a chair for them. That's the most Kenyan, and maybe the most American, thing I know how to do.

From my family to yours: thank you for being part of this story. Whether you've bought one bag, stopped by our booth or are just reading this now, you're at our table.

Asante sana, and happy Thanksgiving.

Martin

If you'd like to share our coffee around your own table this holiday, you can find it in our shop or read more of our family's story.
